plugins.name: Git status
plugins.description: A git indicator in every session's header — a coloured dot and the branch of the repo that session works in, with the uncommitted and unpushed counts on hover, refreshing when the session runs a git command. Click it to review that session's uncommitted changes.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: AC-124: the session-header branch badge now follows a branch switch made outside the session — via an alias, gh, an IDE or an agent tool, none of which print a matching "git checkout" — through a debounced backstop that probes the current branch on other session output, with teardown-safe cleanup.

AC-36: a git-status settings option to hide the branch name in the session-header badge — only the coloured status dot stays on screen (branch name in the tooltip), freeing header width. Default on; updates live.
AC-33: the plugin's icons are drawn from the bundled Material Design set, so they render identically on every machine instead of relying on the OS emoji font.

The branch badge now follows a branch switch made outside the session — another terminal, or the IDE — not only git commands run inside it. It watches the repository's HEAD so a checkout or a deleted branch is reflected within a couple of seconds.
A Browse… button in settings opens a folder picker to add a repository instead of typing its path — it fills the box and adds it in one go. Needs nothing new from the host.

Contributes git steps to a workflow: switch to a branch (creating it), commit, push. It refuses to switch branches with uncommitted work, makes no empty commits, and never forces — force, reset and branch deletion are deliberately absent.

The git status moved out of the sidebar and into each session's own header: a coloured dot and the branch of the repo that session works in, counts on hover, click to drop the summary into that session. A sidebar section could only ever follow the selected session, which said nothing about the other panes on screen. Needs a cockpit build with the session-header contribution point.

Added an inline 'Session repo' panel that follows the active session — the git status of the repo it is working in, refreshing when you switch sessions or the session runs a git command. Needs a cockpit build with the session read/observe surface.
Initial release — per-repo branch / uncommitted / unpushed / ahead-behind via 'git status --porcelain --branch', with inject/copy of a summary.

plugins.name: Prompt Library
plugins.description: A library of reusable prompt templates in the left menu. Click one to insert it into the active session, filling in any {{variable}} fields first. Create, edit and remove templates in the same dialog. Plus a spotlight-style quick-insert (the Ctrl+Shift+P shortcut, or the command palette): a search bar over your prompts — type, then click or Enter to drop one into the session.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: Drawn in the cockpit's colours. The spark in the quick-pick's search bar was still the old orange accent, and the bar itself carried its own fill and edge; both come from the theme now. The list's selected row follows the app's own list styling, which covers the states this plugin's copy did not — a row you had just clicked included.
AC-33: the plugin's icons are drawn from the bundled Material Design set, so they render identically on every machine instead of relying on the OS emoji font.
Deleting a template now asks for confirmation first. Needs a cockpit build with the confirmation dialog.
Quick-insert: subtle hover-grey selection (not the accent), and the search box now takes focus when opened from the shortcut.
Clearer selected-item highlight in the quick-insert list.
Fixed the quick-insert arrow keys not moving the selection.
Fixed the quick-insert search-bar icon rendering as a green emoji on Windows — now a monochrome accent chevron.
The quick-insert is now a spotlight-style search bar (rounded pill + accent icon) instead of a plain box.
Removed the redundant 'Insert prompt' menu button — the quick-insert stays on Ctrl+Shift+P and in the command palette.

Clearer selected-template highlight, plus a quick-insert palette (Insert prompt button / Ctrl+Shift+P) to search and drop a prompt into the session. Needs a cockpit build with the plugin shortcut surface.
Initial release - reusable prompt templates with {{variable}} substitution, click-to-insert into the active session, in-dialog management, five starter templates.

plugins.name: GitHub Issues
plugins.description: Browse open GitHub issues across your repos (via the gh CLI) or one repo in a searchable, sortable dialog, with an "Assigned to me" filter; click one to drop a prompt asking the agent to open and review it — or start it in a new session, which opens the new-session dialog with that prompt ready — and with the cockpit project linked to that repository already selected — so you pick the profile and folder yourself. An issue can also be started in Autopilot (the operator-triggered issue → merge-ready-PR pipeline), which posts its progress back as issue comments. Link a cockpit project to a repository in the project editor, picked from the list gh can see, and this dialog opens on it instead of on every repository you have. Linking an issue to a session you already have open labels that session: it says what it is working on, and takes the issue as its name unless you gave it one yourself. Sessions started under a linked project also run with GH_REPO set to that repository, so a gh command the agent runs is about the repository the project is tracked in rather than whichever one its folder happens to be. The prompt template is editable in settings.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: AC-548: the session picker now respects the repository a session's own project is linked to, instead of searching every repository the owner has.
AC-411: an epic's child issue is now checked against the tracker's own ready-stage and title before Autopilot folds it into a plan.

Drawn in the cockpit's colours. The thin progress line above the list follows the accent rather than a stand-in left over from when it was orange, the labels on an issue take the app's label shape, and the preview and detail boxes round the same way the app's boxes do.

Link a cockpit project to a repository in the project editor, picked from the real list gh can see rather than the repositories that happen to have open issues; the issues dialog then opens on that repository and keeps whatever you pick afterwards.
Sessions started from a GitHub issue are now named after the repository the issue came from (hello-world#42), so the cross-repo view no longer puts two identically named sessions in the sidebar.
Fixes the detail panel showing one issue's heading over another issue's body after a rendering failure, and offering that other issue's prompt for injection (AC-304).

Start an issue in a new session: the new-session dialog opens with the prompt ready, so you pick the profile and folder yourself. Issue descriptions now render as markdown instead of showing raw ## and **. The dialog is rebuilt around a fixed action toolbar, a repository chip and a collapsible prompt preview, in a roomier window. Fixed: the list keeps the issue you were reading while you type, switch repository or toggle Assigned to me; Add to prompt becomes usable as soon as New session has started one; a failed browser launch is reported instead of swallowed; and an expanded prompt preview no longer takes over the whole panel.

AC-216: the Bug fix and Feature templates now mark a run as a code run that ends with a merge-ready pull request, and tell the agent to commit and push its work with clean commits — no Co-Authored-By trailer and no AI/agent mention.
Plan in Autopilot: send a GitHub issue to the Autopilot CEO to plan and run.
Issues can now be started in Autopilot (posts progress back as issue comments); requires host 0.3.0.
AC-33: the plugin's icons are drawn from the bundled Material Design set, so they render identically on every machine instead of relying on the OS emoji font.

Catches up with the plugin as it is built in the repo: the store had 1.7.0 while the manifest had moved on, so an installed copy never saw an update at all. Includes the workflow steps and triggers, and the "assigned to me" filter.

The same session badge and picker as YouTrack, with the actions GitHub actually has: assign to me, label, close as completed or not planned. An issue has no status field, so nothing pretends otherwise. Branch-name pattern and picker search terms are yours to set. Contributes a workflow trigger (issue picked) and steps (pick up, comment, close).
Added an "Assigned to me" filter (gh --assignee @me across repos, or the REST assignee filter for a single repo).
gh CLI + cross-repo, searchable/sortable dialog with a repository filter (All + per-repo), per-field settings help tooltips.
Initial release.

plugins.name: GitHub Pull Requests
plugins.description: Shows how many open GitHub pull requests are yours in the left menu — a button with a live "N / M" badge, your own open PR count next to how many are waiting on your review — refreshing both on a timer and the instant a session opens/merges/closes a PR (it watches session output for a pull url or a merged/closed line), via the gh CLI — the PRs you opened across all your repos, including org repos, or a single repo over HTTP. Clicking it opens a dialog listing every open PR in a searchable, sortable grid with an "Assigned to me" filter, plus a Dashboard widget and a dock-rail panel each showing the same list as a resizable pane with its own item count; left-click a PR to drop a review prompt, or right-click for a menu (add to prompt / open in browser). A pull request that starts waiting for your review raises a toast with an "Open in browser" button. The prompt template is editable in settings.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: Epic AC-448: local runs, the session-facing tools, and the pull-request gate.

Drawn in the cockpit's colours. The thin progress line above the list follows the accent rather than a stand-in left over from when it was orange, and the preview and detail boxes round the same way the app's boxes do.
AC-33: the plugin's icons are drawn from the bundled Material Design set, so they render identically on every machine instead of relying on the OS emoji font.

Adds a GitHub Pull Requests widget for the Dashboard workspace: the same open-PR list as the side-menu section — number, title, repository, an amber stripe on the ones waiting for your review, left-click to drop a review prompt — as a resizable pane with its own item count (1–20). Needs a cockpit build with the dashboard widget system for the widget to appear; the side-menu section works without it.

The list appears in seconds instead of the better part of a minute. The archived-repository list was asked of gh once per owner — three seconds a call, fourteen calls — for an answer already present in the repository list that had just been fetched; those calls are gone. The owner searches now run at once instead of one after another. And the last list is shown the moment the section appears, while the fresh one loads behind it: an empty panel does not read as "loading", it reads as "no open pull requests".

Watch every repository you are involved with — owned, collaborated on, or reached through an organisation — with no list to maintain: gh works out which repositories those are. The list is ordered by last activity, newest first, and the dialog has an Updated column. Right-click a row to set aside a pull request, or every pull request from a repository that is never your business. A loading bar while gh is fetching, and searching no longer brings back what you ignored.

Watch a repository: every open pull request in an owner or an owner/repo, whoever opened it. The searches so far all asked "which of these are mine" — authored by you, assigned to you, waiting on your review — which is the right question for a personal list and the wrong one for a project you are responsible for: five open pull requests in a repo of yours, none of them yours, showed nothing at all. Also: pull requests in archived repositories are excluded everywhere (the exclusion used to apply only when the view was scoped to a single owner, so your own list and your review requests still showed them — and a pull request in an archived repo cannot be merged, reviewed or closed). Plus the workflow templates the previous build shipped.

Contributes an "Open a pull request" step (draft by default) and a "Pull request merged" trigger that fires when one of yours goes in — asked of GitHub every few minutes, and silent on the first look, or every merge you ever made would fire at once.
The inline PR count is now configurable (1-20), and you can limit the list to specific repositories (owner/repo per line; blank = all).
Added a right-click context menu to the inline PR rows: 'Add to prompt' (the normal left-click action) and 'Open in browser'.

Smart refresh — the inline section now also refreshes the instant a session opens, merges or closes a PR, by watching session output for a pull url or a merged/closed line (on top of the 60s timer). Needs a cockpit build with the session read/observe surface.
Added: the inline PR section auto-refreshes (60s) so PRs appear/disappear on their own as they are opened, merged or closed.
Fixed: showed no PRs for the default @me owner — now searches --author @me (your PRs across all repos, including org repos) instead of --owner @me (only repos you own).
Added an "Assigned to me" filter (gh --assignee @me across repos, or a client-side assignees filter for a single repo).
Inline Open PRs section + all-PRs dialog, gh CLI or single-repo HTTP. Hardened JSON parsing; per-field settings help tooltips; settings apply live (no restart).

plugins.name: YouTrack
plugins.description: A left-menu button (or the Shift+Y shortcut) opens a dialog listing open issues across one or more configured YouTrack instances (over HTTP with a permanent token per instance — YouTrack has no CLI), with instance/project/state filters and an "Assigned to me" filter, in a searchable, sortable grid; click one to drop a prompt asking the agent to work on it — or start it in a new session, which opens the new-session dialog with that prompt ready — and with the cockpit project that tracks this YouTrack project already selected — so you pick the profile and folder yourself. Run the ticket workflow from the cockpit: Start an issue (move it to in progress, assign it to you, and tie it to the session you work in), or move it to any state the board itself allows — including workflow-governed boards, whose allowed transitions are read rather than assumed. A linked issue appears with its status in that session's own header, with quick actions (move state, copy branch name, open in browser), and linking one to a session you already have open labels that session: it says what it is working on, and takes the ticket as its name unless you gave it one yourself. An issue can also be started in Autopilot (the operator-triggered issue → merge-ready-PR pipeline), which posts its progress and moves the issue's stage back through this plugin. The prompt template is editable in settings. Link a cockpit project to a YouTrack project in the project editor, picked from the instance's own list, and this dialog opens on it instead of on everything. Also registers each instance's JetBrains remote MCP server so sessions can query YouTrack directly as tools. Screenshots you send with a message are attached automatically to the issue the agent creates or updates that turn (a global setting, on by default).
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: AC-548: the session picker now respects the project a session's own project is linked to, instead of only ever falling back to the instance-wide default.
AC-411: an epic's child issue is now checked against the tracker's own ready-stage and title before Autopilot folds it into a plan.

Drawn in the cockpit's colours. The thin progress line above the list follows the accent rather than a stand-in left over from when it was orange, the labels on an issue take the app's label shape, and the preview and detail boxes round the same way the app's boxes do.

Link a cockpit project to a YouTrack project in the project editor, picked from the instance's own list; the issues dialog then opens on that project instead of on everything, and keeps whatever you pick afterwards.
Fixes the detail panel showing one issue's heading over another issue's description after a rendering failure, and offering that other issue's prompt for injection (AC-304).

Start an issue in a new session: the new-session dialog opens with the prompt ready, so you pick the profile and folder yourself. Issue descriptions now render as markdown instead of showing raw ## and **. The dialog is rebuilt around a fixed action toolbar, a chips strip and a collapsible prompt preview, in a roomier window. Fixed: the result of Start work and Set state no longer disappears the moment it appears; the list keeps the issue you were reading while you type or switch filters; Add to prompt becomes usable as soon as New session has started one; a failed browser launch is reported instead of swallowed; and an expanded prompt preview no longer takes over the whole panel.

AC-212/AC-217: an Epic template that reads a YouTrack epic's child issues (its "parent for" links) and plans them as one coherent run to a single pull request, and the tracker's read-tool MCP servers a source-triggered plan scopes the planning CEO to so it can read the issue and pull an epic's children.
Plan in Autopilot: send a YouTrack issue to the Autopilot CEO to plan and run.
Issues can now be started in Autopilot (posts progress and moves the issue stage); requires host 0.3.0.

AC-116: images you send with a message are attached automatically to the issue the agent creates or updates that turn — a global setting in the plugin settings, on by default. Replaces AC-14's per-session toggle; adds a fallback attach_message_images_to_issue tool.
AC-14: attach images you send with a message to the issue the session tracks — opt-in per session in the header menu.
AC-33: the plugin's icons are drawn from the bundled Material Design set, so they render identically on every machine instead of relying on the OS emoji font.

Plugin-owned MCP (AC-11): the instance's YouTrack MCP server is the plugin's own — it no longer shows in the MCP-servers manager but is offered per-session (uncheckable) in the New-session picker. A per-instance toggle chooses whether an instance contributes its MCP server, and a migration reclaims the entries an earlier version pushed into the registry.

Catches up with the plugin as it is built in the repo (the store stood at 1.10.0, so an installed copy never saw an update): the ticket-status-changed trigger with the statuses read from your board, the workflow templates, and the settings reachable from the dialog itself.

The session header picks the ticket: one menu action per issue tracker instead of a button each, and the badge appears only when a session is actually tracking something. Status moves follow the board's own order — forward, back, or anywhere it allows. The branch-name pattern and which issues the picker shows are yours to set. Contributes a workflow trigger (ticket picked) and a step (set status).
Added a Shift+Y keyboard shortcut that opens the issues dialog (via the new plugin shortcut SDK). Needs a cockpit build with the keyboard-shortcuts system.
Added an "Assigned to me" filter (YouTrack's "for: me" clause added to the query).

Registers the JetBrains remote YouTrack MCP server (/mcp, per configured instance) so a session can query YouTrack via tools. Requires YouTrack Cloud 2026.2+ with the MCP server enabled + a permanent token.
Multiple YouTrack instances; left-menu button opening a dialog with instance/project/state filters (All). Per-field settings help tooltips; no personal instance baked in.
Single-instance per-project open issues over the YouTrack REST API.

plugins.name: Gemini / OpenAI Provider
plugins.description: Adds Gemini and OpenAI as selectable session providers, both over an OpenAI-compatible chat-completions endpoint (Gemini's own OpenAI-compat endpoint, or api.openai.com directly) via Microsoft.Extensions.AI. Runs the session's MCP tools through the cockpit, which gates every call. Configure an API key and model per profile in Manage profiles.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: States plainly that this provider keeps a session's history only while it runs, so a restore offer degrades honestly instead of proposing a resume that would fail.
Applies the host's hidden per-session system prompt (embedded run brief).

Experimental first provider-plugin (#45 phase A): Gemini + OpenAI via the OpenAI-compatible endpoint over Microsoft.Extensions.AI. Trimmed capability flags; API key redacted from ToString; graceful handling when the provider plugin is missing.

plugins.name: Codex (ChatGPT)
plugins.description: Adds the Codex CLI as a provider, in two ways. As a TTY session it runs the real interactive Codex TUI in a pane, the same as Claude's — its own interface, its own approval prompts, which the cockpit cannot see into. As an SDK session it is driven headless, a subprocess per turn (`codex exec --json`); that route has no in-band permission channel at all, because Codex sets approval-policy to never in headless mode. Configure the sandbox per profile. Requires the codex CLI installed and authenticated (`codex login`) on the machine running Cockpit.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: AC-171: fixes the TTY status indicator getting stuck on idle for a Codex session (missing transcript reader, plus an off-by-file-creation-timing bug found in adversarial review), and stops read-aloud from speaking in-progress commentary.
States plainly that a Codex session keeps no conversation you can return to, so a restore offer degrades honestly instead of proposing a resume that would fail.
Carries an MCP server's custom headers through env_http_headers, so the value travels in the environment rather than in a -c argument that every local account can read.
Declares file-access confinement to the working directory (Codex workspace-write), so an isolated Autopilot step on Codex is allowed to run confined.

AC-77 fix: Codex rejected every shared MCP server whose name has a space or colon ("YouTrack: Personal", "SQL Explorer") with "Invalid MCP server name: must match pattern ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$", so 0.4.0 injected the servers but they failed at startup. The server name is now folded to Codex's charset (out-of-set characters become _), so the servers actually start; the Cockpit display name and the Claude route are unchanged.

AC-77: the interactive Codex TUI now receives the session's Cockpit MCP servers as `-c mcp_servers.*` config overrides — previously only the headless app-server route got them, so the TUI saw only its own ~/.codex servers. A bearer token rides the process environment, and a cockpit-hosted server references COCKPIT_MCP_KEY, so no secret lands on the command line.

AC-20: managed provider CLI. The cockpit can install and keep the codex binary up to date in its own location (download → digest verify → extract the release tarball), preferred over PATH yet override-able and removable, with an Install/Update/Remove panel in the profile settings.

AC-40: for a cockpit-hosted MCP the Codex config now points at the COCKPIT_MCP_KEY environment variable (bearer_token_env_var) instead of a literal token, so this run's endpoint key never lands in a config file on disk.

Per-profile environment variables (AC-22): declares SupportsEnvVars and applies the profile's variables to the app-server spawn, laid under the config's own CODEX_HOME/auth so those keep the last word. Also carries the previously unpublished 0.1.2 executable-resolution fallback (~/.local/bin, ~/.bun/bin) for AppImage/GUI launches.
Phase B1: Codex CLI subprocess provider through the plugin session-driver contract (process-per-turn, resume, stderr-drain, interrupt=kill). Live Codex schema/auth/resume verification pending (B2).

plugins.name: GitHub Models
plugins.description: Adds GitHub Models as a selectable session provider, over its OpenAI-compatible chat-completions endpoint (models.github.ai/inference) via Microsoft.Extensions.AI. Runs the session's MCP tools through the cockpit, which gates every call. Configure a GitHub personal access token (models:read scope) and model per profile in Manage profiles. Experimental.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: States plainly that this provider keeps a session's history only while it runs, so a restore offer degrades honestly instead of proposing a resume that would fail.
Applies the host's hidden per-session system prompt (embedded run brief).
GitHub Models via the OpenAI-compatible endpoint over Microsoft.Extensions.AI (same driver as the Gemini/OpenAI provider). Needs a GitHub PAT with models:read.

plugins.name: Claude Transcript Search
plugins.description: Search everything you and the agent ever wrote in a Claude CLI session. Scans the JSONL transcripts of every Claude profile you have configured, opens on the conversations you worked on last so resuming one is a click, and searches back through the rest by any text you or the agent wrote.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: Drawn in the cockpit's colours: the role label on a hit takes the app's label shape, and a result card rounds the same way the app's boxes do.
AC-33: the plugin's icons are drawn from the bundled Material Design set, so they render identically on every machine instead of relying on the OS emoji font.

Resuming a conversation from the search picker now starts the session in the folder it ran in, so it finds that conversation's history instead of opening a fresh one — the picker hands the New-session dialog the working directory alongside the id.

The dialog now opens on the ten conversations you worked on last, each summarised by the prompt you started it with — resuming one is usually a matter of the last few sessions rather than of remembering a word to search for. Clearing the search box returns to that list.

Transcript search moved out of the cockpit's core into this plugin — the JSONL history is Claude's own format, and a multi-provider core has no business parsing it. Keeps the Ctrl+F shortcut and the sidebar button, and adds a picker behind the New-session dialog's Search button so resuming a conversation no longer means typing a session id by hand. Needs a cockpit build with the conversation-picker contribution point.

plugins.name: Workflows
plugins.description: A visual editor for cockpit workflows, and an engine that runs them: drop triggers, actions and decisions on a canvas, wire them together, configure each step, and press Run. Every run is kept — which step got what, what it produced, how long it took — because "it did not work" is not something you can act on. A step this build cannot execute is passed by with a reason, never counted as a success.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: The flow name answers to the pointer and to focus again: it carries a border of its own that stays invisible until you reach for it, now that the cockpit theme no longer lends inputs the stock highlight.

The canvas is retuned. A step's leading stripe says what kind of step it is, and the plain one was a muted blue — fine beside an orange accent, and a near-copy of the accent once that turned blue, so the start of a flow stopped standing out among ordinary steps. It is a neutral slate now. The dotted background, the wire labels, the + handle and the ✕ that removes a connection follow the theme instead of each holding a colour of its own. A failed run is reported in red rather than in the amber this app uses for "waiting for you" — a run that broke is not waiting for anybody.

The Start session step can name the session it opens: fill in Session name and a flow starting a session on a ticket opens it already called after that ticket, instead of opening it as the profile and the clock and renaming it a step later. Leave it empty for the old naming. Needs a cockpit that carries the named start (0.7.0 nightly.59 or later).
Fixes the zoom-in button so the whole zoom toolbar is vector icons (it was still a text '+'), and aligns the plugin's internal version with its manifest.
AC-33: the plugin's icons are drawn from the bundled Material Design set, so they render identically on every machine instead of relying on the OS emoji font.

Security fix (AC-62): the run_workflow MCP tool now refuses a disarmed (inactive) flow, so the operator's arm switch gates the agent route too — an agent can no longer run a flow the operator never armed or deliberately disabled. Running a disarmed flow by hand from the editor is unaffected. Complements the AC-38 consent gate.

AC-40: the cockpit-workflows MCP is the cockpit's own loopback endpoint, so it is no longer listed in the MCP-servers manager; a new toggle in the plugin's own settings view turns it on or off for sessions.

Consent gate (AC-38): a step that acts with your rights — a command, a session hand-off, or egress (http, Slack/Discord) — is put to you for Approve/Deny before it runs, showing the literal action (the command, the URL and body, the full webhook URL). A run you start yourself is never asked; a trigger asks unless you mark the flow Run unattended. An MCP agent cannot create or arm a flow that contains a dangerous step. Plugin-contributed steps declare their own consent in code. Needs a cockpit build from after the AC-38 merge (plugin SDK / Abstractions 1.5.0).

Security fix (AC-39): a value substituted from an earlier step into a command step is shell-quoted, so untrusted step data can no longer break out of its argument and run as a command. Operator templates keep their own shell features.

A workflow MCP (cockpit-workflows) so agents can list, read, run and create/edit workflows through their own tools (AC-12), and a 'Set session status' step that labels the session a flow started with the ticket it picked up (AC-13). Needs a cockpit build with the plugin-MCP endpoint support.
Catches up with the plugin as it is built in the repo (the store stood at 0.18.0): the Switch step, an error exit per step, and templates you can export and import.

First release: a canvas where flows are drawn and an engine that runs them. Triggers that fire by themselves (text in a session, a schedule), steps that use what the steps before produced ({output}, {Step.field}), decisions on real expressions ({= …}), a three-pane node dialog showing what comes in and what came out, run history, and Slack/Discord steps. Other plugins contribute their own steps and triggers.

First release: a canvas where flows are drawn and an engine that runs them. Triggers that fire by themselves (text in a session, a schedule), steps that use what the steps before produced ({output}, {Step.field}), decisions on real expressions ({= …}), a three-pane node dialog showing what comes in and what came out, run history, and Slack/Discord steps. Other plugins contribute their own steps and triggers.

plugins.name: Clock
plugins.description: The time and date, for a Dashboard workspace.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: AC-33: the plugin's icons are drawn from the bundled Material Design set, so they render identically on every machine instead of relying on the OS emoji font.
Initial release — the time and date on a dashboard. Needs a cockpit build with the widget contribution point (AddWidget).

plugins.name: System Monitor
plugins.description: CPU, memory and disk usage for a Dashboard workspace. You pick which of the three in its settings.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: AC-33: the plugin's icons are drawn from the bundled Material Design set, so they render identically on every machine instead of relying on the OS emoji font.
Initial release — CPU, memory and disk on a dashboard, each of the three toggleable per placed instance. Needs a cockpit build with the widget contribution point (AddWidget).

plugins.name: Claude Code
plugins.description: Claude as a provider plugin (Fase 4). Runs the real interactive Claude TUI in a pane (TTY) and, headless, drives it over stream-json (SDK) with the cockpit's permission prompts, live model/permission/effort switching, and usage limits. Bundled and pre-approved: out of the box nothing changes. Requires the claude CLI installed and logged in on the machine running Cockpit.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: TTY sessions now feed their token usage into the cockpit's usage history, same as an SDK session already did.

AC-378: headless (delegated) sessions now get --strict-mcp-config, so they see exactly the resolved MCP servers and never fall back to your own full user/project CLI config. Interactive sessions are unaffected.

The provider now states what its own models cost, cheapest first, so a consumer that routes work by price no longer has to read an order out of a list that never promised one. The figures are estimates and are labelled as such wherever they appear — they are compiled in, not read from a live feed, and can go out of date. Needs cockpit 0.11.0.

Reports the conversation a session is running under, so the cockpit can offer that session back after a crash — and reports it on the terminal route too, where the conversation has to be recognised rather than announced.
Carries an MCP server's custom headers, for a server that wants X-Api-Key or a scheme other than Bearer, alongside the bearer it already sent.
AC-213: the assistant snapshot no longer re-emits the thinking block the stream already sent, so extended reasoning is not rendered twice at the Developer reading level.
Declares file-access confinement to the working directory, so an isolated Autopilot step on Claude is allowed to run confined.
0.4.2 — fix: interleaving TTY and SDK sessions no longer lose their MCP servers (atomic ~/.claude.json trust write)
Fix: pasting an image into a Claude SDK chat session is now attached and sent to the model (the provider registration now declares image/vision support).

AC-20: managed provider CLI. The cockpit can install and keep the claude binary up to date in its own location (download → SHA-256 verify against the release manifest → place), preferred over PATH yet override-able (pin) and removable, with an Install/Update/Remove panel plus an update check in the profile settings.

AC-40: for a cockpit-hosted MCP the Claude mcp-config now references the COCKPIT_MCP_KEY environment variable (Bearer ${COCKPIT_MCP_KEY}) instead of embedding a literal token, so this run's endpoint key never lands in a config file on disk.

Sets COCKPIT_PANE_ID in the SDK spawn's environment (AC-13), so an SDK-session agent can name its own session to the cockpit-session MCP server's set_status tool — the same identity the TTY route already gets. Needs a cockpit build with the cockpit-session MCP.

First store release of the bundled Claude provider. Per-profile environment variables (AC-22): declares SupportsEnvVars and applies the profile's variables to the SDK spawn before the driver's own rules, so ANTHROPIC_* stays dropped and CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR keeps the last word.

plugins.name: GitHub Actions
plugins.description: The GitHub Actions status of the branch a session is working in, shown in that session's header: a coloured dot (green pass, red fail, amber running) for the latest workflow run on the current branch, with the workflow, event and time on hover — click to open the run on GitHub. Completes the GitHub set alongside Issues, Pull Requests and Git status. Uses your existing gh CLI login (no token to paste); requires the GitHub CLI installed and authenticated.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: AC-52: initial release — the GitHub Actions status of the branch a session is working in, shown in that session's header (green pass, red fail, amber running), click to open the run on GitHub.

plugins.name: Session Review
plugins.description: A "Review changes" action in each session's header — and a click on that session's git badge — opens a panel showing what that session changed: a tree of changed files on the left, and on the right one file at a time with old and new line numbers, coloured bands behind changed lines, and the changed words picked out within a replaced line. Untracked files are included, so what a session added is visible too. One click asks the session to review its own changes. Makes the cockpit a review station, not just a runner: the quality guard before an agent's output lands under your name. Requires git installed on the machine running Cockpit.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: The file headers in a diff are lettered in the theme's text colour. They asked for a colour that has never existed under that name, so the lookup could only ever miss and fall through to a flat grey written beside it. Added, removed and hunk lines now track the theme's own green, red and accent rather than near-copies of them.

AC-50: initial release — a Review changes action in each session's header shows the uncommitted git diff of that session's working directory (coloured), with one click to ask the session to review its own changes.

plugins.name: Kubernetes
plugins.description: Register Kubernetes clusters and give agents scoped, human-approved access to them through an mcp__cockpit-k8s__* server. The plugin talks to the cluster itself (via the official Kubernetes client) and keeps the credentials — an agent never gets a kubeconfig. Every call is gated: opening a cluster asks for consent, a namespace outside the cluster's allowed list asks each session (reads included), and every change asks afresh and is never remembered. Cluster-scoped resources, exec and port-forward are off until you turn them on per cluster. A port-forward tunnel shows in the status bar with an operator-only Kill and auto-closes. Configure clusters in the plugin settings: point at a kubeconfig file (e.g. ~/.kube/config, read live) and pick a context from it, or paste a kubeconfig which is stored under the secret layer.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: The warning about a context that authenticates through an external command is drawn in the cockpit's amber rather than a plain orange of its own.

Security fix (AC-92): the exec-consent prompt now escapes newlines and tabs visibly, so a multi-line command cannot masquerade as a single, commented-out line while the raw multi-line command runs against the cluster.
Adds a Sessions-toolbar quick action to open Kubernetes settings (AC-91).

Initial release, hardened after a full code & security review: cluster-scoped consent is remembered per kind (not per cluster), API/exec-auth errors never leak host detail to the agent, a live port-forward survives a settings save, duplicate cluster labels fail closed, and list results flag truncation.

plugins.name: Docker
plugins.description: Register the local Docker daemon and give agents scoped, human-approved access to containers through an mcp__cockpit-docker__* server. The plugin talks to the Docker Engine API itself (via Docker.DotNet) and keeps the connection — an agent never gets the Docker socket. Every call is gated: the first touch of the daemon asks for consent (reads are free after that), and every change (start/stop/remove/run) asks afresh with the literal command shown and is never remembered. Exec is off until you turn it on. Configure the daemon endpoint in the plugin settings (blank uses the local default socket).
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: Rounds out day-to-day dev operations (AC-93): adds logs, compose_logs, list_images, pull_image, inspect, stats, top, list_volumes, list_networks, tag, push, prune, remove_volume, build_image, cp, compose_ps and compose_restart — each with a deliberate consent level (reads free after the one-time daemon consent; changes ask afresh; destructive and exec actions show the target/command). A run against a missing local image now gives a clear 'pull it first' error instead of a misleading daemon-unreachable one.

Initial release: ps/inspect/logs, start/stop/restart/remove, exec and run (behind an off-by-default capability), and Docker Compose up/down/build/config via the CLI — each gated by a human consent prompt that shows the literal command. Sibling of the Kubernetes plugin; built and hardened alongside a full code & security review. Contributes a Sessions-toolbar quick action to open Docker settings (AC-91).

plugins.name: Autopilot
plugins.description: Operator-triggered "issue → merge-ready PR" pipeline. Start a YouTrack or GitHub issue into a visible, self-driving agent session in its own isolated worktree; it works the item behind a quality gate (visual verify, code review, security review, conventions), posts progress and questions back to the issue and moves its stage as it goes, and stops at a merge-ready PR — you approve the run before it starts and always do the merge yourself.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: The reviewing session in an autonomous run is now handed an account of what each step actually changed — produced by the cockpit from the run's own git worktree — instead of being told to distrust the step's summary and re-read the files every time. The step neither writes that account nor can alter it, and it arrives fenced off as data. The cockpit also flags what it can see for itself: work reported while the worktree is unchanged, tests reported passing with nothing test-shaped touched, a step already sent back, a retry after an attempt that ended without a verdict, and a file the step only staged that was already lying there. Where there is nothing to observe — a plain folder with no repository, or a review gate judging rather than changing — the previous full inspection is kept unchanged. Test execution is untouched: no test run is added per step.

The planning brief described a profile's model list as running cheapest-first while it ran the reverse; the roster now follows the order the provider itself declares and says so plainly when a provider declares none. Adds a cost ceiling that is enforced when a plan is submitted rather than merely asked for in the brief: unless the cost strategy is quality-first, a step that is not a review gate must run on the cheaper end of what its profile offers. Run history now records which profile and model ran each step. Needs cockpit 0.11.0.
Epic AC-448: local runs, the session-facing tools, and the pull-request gate.

AC-411: an epic's child is checked against the tracker's own ready-stage and title before it enters an executed plan, in code rather than the CEO's own read of it. (0.11.0 was published under AC-347's content; this corrects the version forward per the immutable-release rule.)

Fixes a broken "Needs you" flow: the pane could keep showing a still-running run while the badge lit up for a different run waiting on you, with no way to reach it. The badge now takes you to the run that needs you (and cycles through several if more than one does), and the blockade panel scrolls so a long question no longer pushes the answer box out of reach.

A run's history now says how many runs in a row settled merge-ready without anything having to be put right, and records per step whether a review sent it back, it ran out of attempts, or you corrected it yourself. A run that ended blocked or stopped, or that never opened the pull request it promised, is not counted as clean. A question the run raised and you answered is counted separately and does not count against it. What the count cannot see from the inside — a review finding an agent repairs within its own step — is stated on the figure itself, and any classification can be corrected by right-clicking the step.

Review gates now spend their verification where the verdict is: while a gate is still finding things it builds incrementally and runs the tests around the change, and only the round that finds nothing does the whole-project build with warnings as errors and the complete test suite. Each round is asked to report what it actually built and ran, and the same requirement goes into the gate's acceptance. Also in this version: the Autopilot planner opens once — asking for it again brings the window you have forward instead of building a second one — and its settings window is one per plugin.
A run's sessions now carry the run they belong to, so what a run spent can be added up afterwards.

Drawn in the cockpit's colours. The Continue, Approve and Send buttons and the Cancel beside them are the app's own buttons now rather than hand-mixed copies, so they carry the same fill, corner and padding as every other dialog. The "needs you" badge, the "the CEO is working…" band and the number inside a step's dot were lettered in a near-black mixed for the old orange accent; they sit on bright fills and now use the colour the theme has for exactly that. The profile and model chips take the app's label shape.
Fixes the CEO validator being refused by the tightened confinement gate, and a run hanging when its reviewing CEO cannot start.

AC-212/AC-214/AC-215/AC-216/AC-217: Autopilot takes a code run to a merge-ready pull request (commit, push, open the PR — you still do the merge), with an up-front preflight when it cannot; an Epic template that plans a YouTrack epic's child issues as one run to a single PR; the planning CEO scoped to the tracker's read tools; the "CEO is working" cue as a full-width top bar; and an autonomous run that no longer stalls on permission prompts — its own control tools are pre-authorized and, isolated in a worktree, it runs its work tools without prompting, with an activity-aware step stall so a slow-but-working step is not failed as stuck.

Name the folder an Autopilot run works in — pick a recent/pinned folder or browse, and the CEO can propose it. A git repository isolates each step in a worktree; a plain folder (an admin task with no repo) now runs in it directly, confined to that folder, instead of failing at the first step.

Autopilot CEO: plan a run, approve once, autonomous to merge-ready — each step in the run's own worktree on the model you pick (incl. confined local models), code+security review gates, queue and history, Plan in Autopilot from YouTrack/GitHub.
First full release of Autopilot: the operator-triggered issue → merge-ready-PR pipeline (needs host 0.3.0).

First release: an example of a full-surface workspace a plugin draws end to end, with a real host session embedded in it — a reference for the AC-122 workspace-type API.

plugins.name: Kimi Code Provider (ACP)
plugins.description: Adds Kimi Code as a session provider, driven over the Agent Client Protocol (JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio) via `kimi acp` — a persistent process for the whole session, with streaming text/thinking, tool calls and live permission prompts. Requires the kimi CLI installed and authenticated on this machine (an API key, or `kimi acp --login`); the cockpit resolves `kimi` from PATH or a pinned path you set, it does not install it for you. Three known limitations: Kimi maps a failed turn to the same stopReason as a successful one, so this provider cannot tell the two apart from the wire alone; Kimi reports no quota or cost, so the session shows a context percentage but no rate-limit windows; and `kimi acp` has no way to receive a system prompt, so a profile identity or project instruction is not applied — the session says so in the transcript rather than dropping it silently.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: Carries an MCP server's custom headers in its headers array, alongside the bearer it already sent.

Initial release — Kimi Code over the Agent Client Protocol: streaming text and thinking, tool calls with real Allow/Deny prompts, live model/mode/thinking switching, resume and cancel, and the cockpit's MCP servers handed to the child. Needs the kimi CLI on PATH (or a pinned path) and an API key or its own login. Three documented limits: a failed turn is indistinguishable from a successful one, there is no quota or cost to report, and a system prompt cannot be handed to Kimi — the session says so instead of dropping it.

plugins.name: Local CI
plugins.description: Runs your GitHub workflow jobs on this machine's own Docker, from the session that is working on the code. It reports Docker in three states rather than two — missing, installed but the engine is not answering, or ready — checks that the engine runs Linux containers, and says whether the act runtime is on PATH, naming the install command when it is not. It reads the project's .github/workflows and says, per job, either that it can run here or the concrete reason it cannot: a matrix, a runner that is not Linux, artifacts exchanged with another job, or an action that only means something on GitHub. A job runs whole or not at all — anything it does not understand it refuses rather than guesses. A session can start a run itself and read the verdict back, with the operator approving the exact command each time, and a project can be set to hold back its pull requests until a local run has passed. The verdict is about this machine: act's images are not GitHub's, so it predicts the pull-request check rather than replacing it.
plugins.author: Cockpit

versions.notes: Epic AC-448: local runs, the session-facing tools, and the pull-request gate.

First release. Reports whether this machine can run a workflow job locally — Docker in three states, Linux containers, the act runtime — and says per job whether it can run locally or the concrete reason it cannot.

plugins.name: Depot
plugins.description: Lets a project's memory live in a Depot project instead of a folder, and connects one or more Depot instances so a session can reach them.
plugins.author: Cockpit

Requires host 0.10.0.

Runs the session's MCP tools through the cockpit, which gates every call. Configure an xAI API key and model (e.g. grok-4.6) per profile in Manage profiles. Experimental.

plugins.author: Cockpit

plugins.name: opencode Provider (ACP)
plugins.description: Adds opencode as a session provider, driven over the Agent Client Protocol (JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio) via `opencode acp` — a persistent process for the whole session, with streaming text/thinking, real tool calls and live permission prompts routed through Cockpit's own consent card. Requires the opencode CLI installed on this machine (opencode.ai/docs); most models also need authentication (an API key, or `opencode auth login`) though opencode's own free-tier models need neither. Live usage/cost figures stream per turn over ACP's usage_update notification. opencode has no way to receive a system prompt over ACP, so a profile identity or project instruction is not applied — the session says so in the transcript rather than dropping it silently.
plugins.author: Cockpit

plugins.name: Diagram, Whiteboard & Wireframe
plugins.description: Opens a Mermaid diagram in its own window, bound to a session you already have running, a whiteboard window you can invite that session's agent to look along on — and, if you approve it, to draw along on — and now a wireframe sketch window coupled the same way.
plugins.author: Cockpit

plugins.author: Cockpit

plugins.description: Talk to your assistant from Slack — a second door onto the same conversation the chat window shows.

plugins.name: Proxmox VE
plugins.description: Register a Proxmox VE host or cluster and give agents scoped, human-approved access to its nodes, VMs and LXC containers through an mcp__cockpit-proxmox__* server. The plugin talks to the Proxmox REST API itself and keeps the API token — an agent never gets it. Connecting asks for consent once (reads are free after that), and every change (start/stop/shutdown/reboot/snapshot) asks afresh with the literal action shown and is never remembered. Rolling back a snapshot and deleting a VM or LXC container are off until you turn them on. Self-signed certificates are trusted only after you confirm the shown fingerprint in the plugin settings.
plugins.author: Cockpit

templates.author: Cockpit
